The ATT estimate is **0.060**, using the doubly robust (AIPW) estimator.

**Data:** 2,570 rows, 246 treated and 2,324 controls. The outcome `y` is binary (employment status, mean 0.847), so the ATT is a difference in employment probability.

**Method:** I fit a logistic propensity model on x0–x16 with an intercept. The AIPW ATT is the mean of `t·(y − μ₀(x))` over the treated, minus the propensity-weighted mean of `(1−t)·p/(1−p)·(y − μ₀(x))` over the controls, all divided by the treated share. Here μ₀ is a logistic outcome model fit on controls. Its outcome model and propensity model are both correct only in the sense that they are the standard logistic specifications, so the estimate is only as good as those specifications.

**Robustness:** The other estimators are close, but the spread is worth knowing:

| Estimator | ATT |
|---|---|
| Naive difference in means | −0.101 |
| IPW (normalized, ATT weights) | 0.063 |
| Outcome regression (logit) | 0.073 |
| Outcome regression (OLS) | 0.067 |
| **AIPW (reported)** | **0.060** |
| 1-NN propensity matching | 0.024 |
| 5-NN propensity matching | 0.035 |
| 1-NN standardized covariate matching | 0.037 |

The naive comparison is negative because the treated group differs from the controls on the covariates. Once those are adjusted for, the effect is positive. The matching estimates are noisier, since they use only a handful of controls per treated unit, and they fall below the model-based estimates. I didn't compute standard errors, so I can't say how much of the gap between 0.024 and 0.073 is sampling noise.

ANSWER: 0.060
